messages.subject: Height of nodes in snow model
messages.subject_clean: Height of nodes in snow model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question about the heights above ground for which snow
temperatures are returned (as in e.g. sunsnow when running [microclimate()]).

In short: how does one get from SN1..9 to a height above ground?

In long: are heights for SN1..9 a fixed fraction of total snow depth (i.e time variant)? Are they equally spaced? Is 1 or 9 lower? Do they represent snow layer temperatures or heat exchange node temperatures (and if node temperatures does 9 nodes = 8 layers or is the lowest node not included as it is effectively the soil surface temperature).

I couldn't find anything on this in the help files or vignettes. Apologies if it is there.

Best wishes,

Ilya Maclean

Associate Professor of Global Change Biology

University of Exeter Penryn campus
www.exeter.ac.uk <http://www.exeter.ac.uk/>
Environment and Sustainability Institute, Penryn Campus, Penryn, Cornwall, TR10
9FE

messages.subject_clean: Conversion of Critical Leaf Water Threshold and estimation of other Vegetation Parameters (micro_ncep)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew, Mike,

Yes - microclimc is your friend here. (install_github("ilyamaclean/microclimc"). I've integrated it with NicheMapR, such that it uses NicheMapR to do soil / snow modelling, but calls a separate function for doing below-canopy microclimate conditions including relative humidity. The runwithNMR function does this and will return local relative humidity accounting for soil (and leaf) evapotranspiration.

The model is still under development, the paper describing methods not published yet, and it isn't entirely 100% glitch free. It should work though

Ilya

messages.subject: Re: Height of nodes in snow model
messages.subject_clean: Height of nodes in snow model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ilya,

I should probably put that into the help and vignettes but it's described in this paper:

Kearney, M.R. (2020) How will snow alter exposure of organisms to cold stress under climate warming? Global Ecology and Biogeography 29, 1246–1256.

"Snow layers form an extension of a maximum of eight nodes above the ten nodes used to compute heat flux through the soil profile. These additional snow nodes are at 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 300cm, with the original soil surface node (0cm) acting as the snow surface node and the connection between the 300cm snow node and the depth of the soil surface node being allowed to grow to an arbitrary large extent. As the snow pack grows and shrinks, the subroutine ‘snowlayer’ checks whether to increase or decrease the number of snow nodes in use. Snow is set to zero if the predicted depth is less than 2.5 cm to ensure numerical stability but small rainfall events that would otherwise produce a snow layer shallower than this threshold are cumulated each hour until the threshold is met, conserving mass balance"

So with the snow temperature output and the snow depth for each hour, you should have the answer - they are fixed in their spacing aside from the bottom node which varies as the snow pack grows to depths in between the fixed nodes.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Height of nodes in snow model
messages.subject_clean: Height of nodes in snow model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ilya,

Yes TALOC (and VLOC, RHLOC) is at whatever the local height is set to with Usrhyt, above the snow surface, and the wind speed and air temp profiles are adjusted from the snow surface upwards with exchange being based on snow surface temperature. But that also means that the reference height is effectively rising (in terms of height above the actual ground) as the snow pack grows.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: minshade vs minshades clarification
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Apologies if this has already been addressed, and I missed it. My colleague and I are in the early stages of developing our model and are having trouble figuring out the explicit difference between minshade and minshades and how they're applied in the context of the ectotherm model.

Additionally, we are wondering what shade value is used in the ectotherm model if all behavioral parameters are set to 0 (e.g. a non-thermoregulating ectotherm). We have two environments of very different min and max shade values (which are set in the inputs) but have outputs that look identical. We are struggling to identify the disconnect.

Any help understanding these details would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you.

messages.subject: Re: minshade vs minshades clarification
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sidney,

Good questions. Originally you could only set a single value for minshade and maxshade for both the microclimate model and the ectotherm model. I subsequently added the facility of including time-varying shade (on a daily basis, e.g. to capture changes in vegetation structure) but kept the original input parameters for fixed shade, and just had the code create a vector of daily values on the fly if the user wasn't specifying time-varying shade. Your comment made me realise that this is a bit confusing. So,  I've made the following changes (now pushed to github):

1. For the microclimate model functions (e.g. micro_global, micro_usa, etc.), 'minshade' and 'maxshade' can be single values (constant through time) or a vector of daily values (which you can make variable through time, e.g. to simulate a fire). If you put single values, the code will internally convert them into a vector of daily values and the outputs 'minshade' and 'maxshade' from the function will be the vector of daily values.

2. For the ectotherm model, the 'minshade' input parameter is now gone, and it just has 'minshades' and 'maxshades' which, by default, are taken from the microclimate output list on the assumption that you've called this list 'micro', i.e. 'micro$minshade' and 'micro$maxshade'. But, you can override these if you wish with a different vector of shade values. This could be because, for example, you've simulated the microclimate of a forest floor where shade might be 90%, but you want to simulate an animal tracking a sun spot. Or, you might have simulated an animal in an unshaded microclimate but you want to simulate it sitting in the shade of a small object in that environment. So, in the first case the microclimate in terms of air temperature, ground temperature, sky temperature, humidity and wind speed is that of a forest floor, but the animal is receiving full sun from the sun spot. And vice versa for the second case.

Note also that the solar radiation returned by the microclimate model in 'metout' and 'shadmet' (column 'SOLR') is unshaded - this is so that the ectotherm model has the unshaded values available to it so you can run simulations of the type I just described, e.g. the sun spot example of experiencing 0% shade in a microclimate that is 90% shaded. I've now added a message to this effect in the microclimate functions. The thing to be mindful of here, though, is that the air temperature, sky temperature and ground temperature get adjusted by a weighting relating to the current shade value compared to the maximum one. E.g.

       TA = TA_MINSHADE*((MAXSHD-SHADE)/MAXSHD) +  TA_MAXSHADE *(SHADE/MAXSHD)

with MAXSHADE being the value for the day that you inputted via the 'maxshades' vector and SHADE being the value the model is currently using via the behavioural thermoregulation algorithm in the ectotherm model. I know all this is a bit complex, but so are microclimates and animals behaving in them :).

To answer your second question, if you set the simulation up so the animal can't thermoregulate, it will use the minimum shade microclimate. So if you want to simulate a non-thermoregulating animal under different shade levels, you want to vary 'minshade' in the microclimate model. Note also that there is the parameter 'live' which you can set to zero and the animal will be stuck on the surface in the minimum shade environment. Note that this setting turns of any metabolic heat generation (usually trivial for an ectotherm) or respiratory water loss, but cutaneous water loss still occurs.

If you're still not getting the outputs you expect from your simulations of different shade levels, post the code here and I'll take a look.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: micro_era5
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I've just added a new function 'micro_era5' to NicheMapR. It allows you to run the microclimate model with the powerful new data set ERA5 <https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/datasets/reanalysis-datasets/era5> from the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) <https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/#!/search?text=ERA5&type=dataset>. This was made possible by James Duffy's package mcera5 <https://github.com/everydayduffy/mcera5>. There's an example of how to use it, including the first step of downloading a time/space slice of the ERA5 data with mcera5, in the examples section of the help for this function.

Let me know if you find any issues with it.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: NicheMapR v. 3.0.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I put out a new release of NicheMapR <https://zenodo.org/record/4146966#.X7MQZYtxVaQ> recently - timed with a forthcoming paper in Methods in Ecology and Evolution on modelling body size effects on thermoregulation with the transient heat budget functions onelump, onelump_var and twolump. I'll let you know when that paper comes out.

Also in that release is the endotherm model 'endoR', which is now fully described and open source. There are a number of vignettes in the package on the endotherm model too. Of course, as soon as I released it we found an issue with conduction in the endoR_devel and endoR functions, which is now corrected on the current version in github. I'll fix this in the next release, which will be timed with the software note for the endotherm model (currently in review).

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: microclimate model crashing on Macs
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I've now had a couple of reports of the micro_ functions crashing on some Macs and I found this to be the case on mine.

It is due to the 'gads' program, a Fortran routine that reads in data from a global aerosol database that I've included in the NicheMapR package.

After a full day of pain, I found where the crash happens (where it tries to open a file for reading) but I see no obvious way around. So, I've coded the entire program in R and included it as a new function - gads.r - in the package. It is now on github and I'll include it in the next release.

So, when running the micro_ functions, e.g. micro_global, micro_ncep, etc., you can now include the option 'run.gads = 2' and it will use the R version of gads. This is a bit slower but is the best solution I can come up with for this odd issue.

Not sure how many of you have had this problem as yet. If you do run into it, I'd be curious to know what OS and version of R you are running.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Cooler and moister mesoclimatic conditions, but warmer and drier microclimatic conditions at the same time?
messages.subject_clean: Cooler and moister mesoclimatic conditions, but warmer and drier microclimatic conditions at the same time?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I would like to ask for an apparent contradiction between mesoclimate and microclimatic variables calculated with micro_ncep and ectotherm variables calculated with ectotherm.

I calculated data for 105 points between two adjacent zones (A and B). Zone A had a higher altitude, vegetation cover (estimated as NDVI), as well as lower temperature and relative humidity in mesoclimatic conditions (TAREF and RH [2m]). However, the same zone A resulted in higher microclimatic temperature and relative humidity (TALOC and RHLOC [0.03cm]), as well as higher body temperature (TC) and substrate (TSUB), greater use of shade (SHADE), and higher metabolism (O2_ml).

 I analyzed the substrate temperature at a 30m scale with a substrate temperature raster obtained via MODIS. We found that for the same study points, the substrate temperature was higher in zone B than in A, contrary to the microclimatic—but consistent with the mesoclimatic—results obtained with NicheMapR.

So my question is how can mesoclimatic conditions be cooler and moister in zone A, but at the same time, microclimatic conditions be hotter and drier in the same zone?

I attach an example to obtain data for 10 geographic points by each zone (IVE_Template_301120). In the database, zone A refers to DENTRO and B to NORTE. Since I am controlling for the effect of climate differences, I compare two years with different vegetation cover but experiencing the climate conditions of the hottest year in Mexico (2017).

Thank you very much for your time.

messages.body_plain:
I have a question regarding the SOLR output. I recognize that for both the shade and unshaded (metout and shadmet) output in the micro_global function the SOLR output is calculated for an unshaded horizontal plane. Is there a way of calculating solar radiation under shaded conditions (the specified shade values) as well?

Thank you!
Adam

messages.subject: Re: Cooler and moister mesoclimatic conditions, but warmer and drier microclimatic conditions at the same time?
messages.subject_clean: Cooler and moister mesoclimatic conditions, but warmer and drier microclimatic conditions at the same time?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Israel,

To really work out what's going on, you'd have to compare the inputs and outputs at particular sites, e.g. two contrasting sites from your two zones. More generally, the NCEP data is at ~2 degrees resolution and you're looking at points within about 0.5 degrees so you may have one or two pixels of NCEP depending on where the points lie on the grid. That means that you may have a sudden jump in the variables that aren't being adjusted by the micro_ncep function, e.g. rainfall, cloud cover. Differences in cloud cover are the most likely reason you'd see a higher microclimatic temperature at a site with a lower 2m air temp. I see you're using NDVI as maximum shade - it isn't really a measure of shade but would be proportional to shade. Be careful comparing relative humidity - it's a function of temperature. Better to compute vapour pressure (use the WETAIR function) to see if the air is truly moister.

Re the ectotherm model - try turning all behaviour off and see what you get. Also, some notes on the parameters you've used:

fossorial = 0 # this isn't properly implemented yet so don't turn it on

rainact = 1 # you have set activity to be limited by rainfall which could also be affecting your Tb estimates, depending on whether you have more than one pixel of NCEP data overlapping

All the parameters below are relevant only if the DEB model is running

T_REF= 34.2+273.15, # soilnode = 1, eggshade = 1, T_L = 30.6+273.15, T_H = 36.4+273.15, stage = 2, viviparous = 0, photostart = 4, photofinish = 1, photodirs = 0
Hope that helps,
Mike
